chunks: What a real-time operating system is. The question: What is a real-time operating system (RTOS)?
A real-time operating system (RTOS) is an OS built so that its timing is predictable. Real-time does not mean fast.
It means that the worst-case response is bounded and known, so tasks meet their deadlines reliably.
It does this mainly with a scheduler that always runs the most urgent ready task.
Compare two trains. One is slow but always runs to a fixed timetable. The other is fast but arrives whenever it likes. If you must catch a connection, you want the first.
A real-time system is the timetable train: what matters is that it is never later than the promised limit, not how fast it is on a good day.
Each column is 1 milliseconds; a high level means the task is running. T1 always runs the moment it is released. T2 runs in the first gaps (1 to 3 milliseconds).
T3 gets the CPU only in the remaining gaps: 3 to 5 milliseconds, then is preempted at 5 milliseconds by T1, and finishes at 7 milliseconds (its worst-case response time).
The CPU is idle from 7 to 10 milliseconds.
Deadline: the time by which a result must be ready. Hard real-time: missing a deadline is a failure, as with an airbag controller.
Soft real-time : occasional misses just lower quality, like a dropped video frame. Preemption: pausing a running task so a more urgent one can run at once.
Worst case: the longest the response could ever take, which is the number real-time design cares about.
OS: ("What an operating system is"): software that manages the CPU, memory and devices for programs.
A control task must run every 1 milliseconds, and a logging task runs whenever it has data. Give the control task the higher priority.
The logging task is running when the 1 milliseconds timer fires and makes the control task ready. The scheduler pauses logging within a few microseconds and runs the control task.
So the control task's worst-case delay is that short switch time, plus any short moments when interrupts are off.
Even so, you must still check that all the tasks fit, because the RTOS does not guarantee deadlines by itself. That is the whole idea.
"A real-time OS is one whose timing is predictable: real-time means meeting deadlines reliably, not being fast.
It uses a priority-based preemptive scheduler, so the highest-priority ready task runs within a bounded, small latency, with short, bounded interrupt-disabled sections and deterministic primitives.
Hard real-time means a miss is a failure; soft means degraded. FreeRTOS, Zephyr, VxWorks and QNX are examples.
The RTOS enables real-time, but I still must analyse schedulability and avoid priority inversion."
